title: Members of the Medical Licensing Board of Indiana v. Planned Parenthood Great Northwest
description: Whether the Indiana Supreme Court should grant the petition to transfer jurisdiction from the Court of Appeals regarding the case involving Planned Parenthood and the Medical Licensing Board.
plaintiff_argument: Planned Parenthood, as the appellant, sought to have the Indiana Supreme Court review their case by filing a petition to transfer jurisdiction.
defendant_argument: The Members of the Medical Licensing Board of Indiana, as appellees, implicitly argued against the transfer of jurisdiction, supporting the Court of Appeals' decision.
decision_outcome: The Indiana Supreme Court denied the petition to transfer jurisdiction, meaning the Court of Appeals' decision stands.

title: Ward v. State
description: Whether Roy Lee Ward should be granted leave to file a successive post-conviction relief petition to challenge his method of execution and whether an execution date should be set before his public records requests are resolved.
plaintiff_argument: Ward argues he should be allowed to file a successive PCR petition to challenge the constitutionality of his lethal injection protocol and execution chamber conditions, and that the State's failure to provide public records obstructs his ability to do so, violating his due process and Eighth Amendment rights.
defendant_argument: The State argues Ward has no further grounds for review, his claims about the execution method do not challenge the validity of his conviction or sentence, and therefore, his request for successive PCR should be denied and an execution date should be set.
decision_outcome: The court denied Roy Lee Ward's request to seek successive post-conviction relief and ordered his execution to be carried out on October 10, 2025.

title: J.F. v. St. Vincent Hospital
description: Whether a timely appeal of a temporary civil commitment becomes moot when the commitment ends, and whether there was sufficient evidence to support J.F.'s temporary commitment.
plaintiff_argument: J.F. argued that her appeal should not be dismissed as moot despite her commitment expiring, and that there was insufficient clear and convincing evidence to support the finding that she was gravely disabled.
defendant_argument: St. Vincent Hospital implicitly argued that the commitment was valid and supported by clear and convincing evidence that J.F.'s deterioration left her unable to function independently and put herself and her children in danger.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the temporary commitment order, ruling that such appeals generally do not become moot upon expiration unless the appellee establishes the absence of collateral consequences, and found sufficient evidence supported J.F.'s commitment.

title: Jackson v. State
description: Whether a warrantless search of a car's locked trunk, based solely on the smell of burnt marijuana from the passenger compartment, violates constitutional rights against unreasonable searches.
plaintiff_argument: The warrantless search of his trunk, based only on the smell of burnt marijuana, violated his rights under Article 1, Section 11 of the Indiana Constitution.
defendant_argument: The smell of burnt marijuana provided probable cause for the officer to conduct a warrantless search of the entire car, including the locked trunk, making the search reasonable.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court denied the petition to transfer jurisdiction, thereby upholding the Court of Appeals' decision that affirmed the trial court's denial of Jackson's motion to suppress the evidence.

title: Indiana Bureau of Motor Vehicles v. Simmons
description: Whether the phrase "biological division of being either female or male" in a previous court opinion should be modified by removing the word "biological".
plaintiff_argument: The Appellees argued that the phrase "biological division of being either female or male" has no support in usage or law and will be used to harm transgender individuals, requesting its removal.
defendant_argument: The Appellants implicitly argued against removing the word "biological" from the phrase, as it was part of the original decision they prevailed in.
decision_outcome: The court granted the rehearing and modified its opinion by striking the word "biological" from the phrase "biological division of being either female or male", while reaffirming its original decision in all other respects.

title: Cosme v. Clark
description: Whether a court may take on the jury's fact-finding role to weigh evidence and assess witness credibility at the close of the plaintiff's case, or if it must only review whether inferences from the evidence are reasonable without weighing conflicting evidence or assessing credibility.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that courts should not weigh conflicting evidence or assess witness credibility at the directed-verdict stage, as doing so infringes on the constitutional right to a jury trial.
defendant_argument: The defendant implicitly argued that courts can weigh evidence and assess witness credibility at the directed-verdict stage to determine if sufficient evidence supports a claim.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the trial court's directed verdict for Erie Insurance Exchange, allowing the Cosmes' claims against Erie to proceed, but affirmed the directed verdict for Churilla Insurance, dismissing claims against Churilla.

title: Mellowitz v. Ball State University
description: Whether Public Law No. 166-2021, which prohibits class action lawsuits against postsecondary educational institutions for contract or unjust enrichment claims arising from COVID-19, is constitutional.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff, Keller Mellowitz, argued that the law is unconstitutional because it violates the separation of powers by usurping judicial authority over class actions, constitutes an unconstitutional taking of property (the right to a class action), and impairs his contract with Ball State University.
defendant_argument: The defendants, Ball State University and the State of Indiana, argued that the law is constitutional as it predominantly furthers a public policy objective, does not unconstitutionally take Mellowitz's property (as he has no property right to a class action), and does not impair his contract (as his individual claims are preserved).
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the trial court's order, ruling that Mellowitz may pursue his individual claims against Ball State University but cannot pursue a class action on behalf of other students, finding the law constitutional.

title: State v. $2,435 in United States Currency
description: Whether the right to a jury trial applies in an action seeking to confiscate money under Indiana's civil forfeiture statute.
plaintiff_argument: The State argues that there is no right to a jury trial in civil forfeiture cases because they are purely statutory procedures and are equitable, not legal, in nature.
defendant_argument: Kizer argues that the right to a jury trial applies in civil forfeiture cases, tracing this right to common-law in rem procedures with jury trials that existed historically.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the trial court's decision, ruling that a claimant in an action brought under Indiana's civil forfeiture statute has a constitutional right to a trial by jury.

title: State v. Kizer
description: Whether a claimant in an action brought under Indiana's civil forfeiture statute has a constitutional right to trial by jury.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that no right to a jury trial exists in civil forfeiture cases because they are special statutory procedures of modern vintage, not common law actions.
defendant_argument: Kizer argued that civil actions to forfeit property used in violation of law have historical roots in common-law courts with jury trials, and denying a jury trial would unduly restrict constitutional rights.
decision_outcome: The court held that a claimant in an action brought under Indiana's civil forfeiture statute has a constitutional right to trial by jury, affirming the trial court's decision to remand for a jury trial.

title: Harris v. State
description: Whether a defendant in a habitual offender proceeding has a constitutional right to present testimony regarding the circumstances of their crimes and rehabilitation efforts to persuade the jury on their habitual offender status, or if the jury's role is limited to determining the existence of prior convictions.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the habitual offender statute, as amended, limits the jury's role to determining only the existence of prior unrelated convictions, making Harris's proffered testimony irrelevant to that determination.
defendant_argument: Harris argued that Article 1, Section 19 of the Indiana Constitution grants the jury the right to determine both the facts and the law, allowing them to decide whether he was ultimately a habitual offender, and thus his testimony about his circumstances was relevant to this determination and to seek mercy.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the trial court's exclusion of Harris's testimony and upheld the determination of his habitual offender status, ruling that only evidence proving or disproving prior convictions is relevant in such proceedings.

title: Holcomb v. Bray
description: Whether the General Assembly can constitutionally authorize its Legislative Council to call an emergency session by simple resolution when the General Assembly is not in session, or if this power is exclusively vested in the Governor and requires a properly enacted law.
plaintiff_argument: The Governor argued that HEA-1123 is unconstitutional because it grants the Legislative Council the power to call an emergency session by resolution when the General Assembly is not in session, thereby usurping a power exclusively granted to the Governor under Article 4, Section 9, violating the distribution of powers (Article 3, Section 1), and circumventing constitutional amendment requirements (Article 16).
defendant_argument: The Legislative Parties argued that HEA-1123 is a lawful exercise of the General Assembly's constitutional authority to set its own meeting times, and the General Assembly may set "by law" whatever rules it wishes to govern the timing of its sessions.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that HEA-1123 is unconstitutional because it violates Article 4, Section 9's fixed-by-law requirement by allowing an emergency session to be set by simple resolution, and it infringes on the Governor's exclusive constitutional authority to call a special session, thereby violating Article 3, Section 1's distribution-of-powers mandate. The court also found the Governor was not procedurally barred from bringing the suit.

title: State v. Katz
description: Whether Indiana Code section 35-45-4-8, which criminalizes the non-consensual distribution of intimate images, is constitutional under the Indiana Constitution's free expression clause and the First Amendment's free speech clause.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued the statute is constitutional, not unconstitutionally overbroad, and serves a compelling state interest in protecting privacy, while being narrowly tailored to address the problem of nonconsensual pornography.
defendant_argument: Katz argued the statute is unconstitutional under both the Indiana Constitution (Article 1, Section 9) and the First Amendment (overbroad, content-based restriction failing strict scrutiny), and that the State failed to allege an offense.
decision_outcome: The Indiana Supreme Court reversed the trial court's dismissal, finding the statute constitutional under both the Indiana Constitution and the First Amendment, and remanded the case for further proceedings.

title: City of Bloomington Board of Zoning Appeals v. UJ-Eighty Corp.
description: Whether the City of Bloomington impermissibly delegated its zoning authority to Indiana University by defining fraternities and sororities based on their relationship with the university, thereby violating state and federal constitutional due process rights.
plaintiff_argument: UJ-Eighty argued that Bloomington unlawfully delegated its zoning authority to IU, allowing IU to unilaterally define fraternities and sororities without oversight, which violated state and federal constitutional due process rights.
defendant_argument: The City of Bloomington Board of Zoning Appeals argued that Bloomington did not delegate authority but rather defined fraternities and sororities in its zoning law based on their relationship with IU, and therefore, no constitutional violations occurred.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Indiana reversed the trial court's judgment, concluding that Bloomington did not improperly delegate zoning authority to IU and did not violate UJ-Eighty's due process rights.
